parts.title: Booking a restaurant for a family celebration
parts.context: A woman phones a restaurant to reserve a table for her parents' anniversary.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a restaurant to book a table for a family celebration. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: The Olive Tree Restaurant, Dan speaking.

script.speaker: elena
script.text: Hello. I'd like to reserve a table for a family dinner. My parents are celebrating a special occasion.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: How lovely. Let me take some details, and then we can talk about what you need.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The booking is for a family dinner, so 'dinner' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: elena
script.text: Elena Petrova. That's P-E-T-R-O-V-A.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Thank you, Ms Petrova. What's the occasion?

script.speaker: elena
script.text: It's my parents' fortieth wedding anniversary. They got married in a tiny church in Poland, and they've never had a proper party.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: That deserves a good table. And the date?

script.speaker: elena
script.text: Saturday the eighteenth of October, if you have space.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: We do. How many guests will there be?

script.speaker: elena
script.text: I thought fourteen, but two cousins can't come now, so it'll be twelve.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: And what time would you like? We have tables from six.

script.speaker: elena
script.text: Half past six was my first idea, but my uncle works late on Saturdays, so could we say seven?

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Seven is fine.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Now, any requests? Would you like a particular table?

script.speaker: elena
script.text: If possible, one near the window, because there's a lovely view of the river.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: I can't promise the fireplace table, as that is already booked, but the window table is free, and it's large enough for twelve.

script.speaker: elena
script.text: The window is perfect. One more thing: my aunt is allergic to shellfish, so we need to be careful.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: I'll tell the chef, and we'll make a note on the booking.

script.speaker: elena
script.text: Also, may I bring my own cake? My mother's sister has baked one.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Of course. We don't charge for that, and we'll bring plates and knives.

script.speaker: elena
script.text: Wonderful. Do I need to pay anything now?

script.speaker: dan
script.text: For groups of more than ten we ask for a deposit. It's usually a hundred pounds, but for a table of twelve, fifty is enough. We ask you to pay it within three days, to keep the reservation.

script.speaker: elena
script.text: That's fine. I'll do it tomorrow.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Lovely. We look forward to seeing you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A new reptile house
parts.context: A keeper welcomes visitors to a new reptile house at a zoo.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to a new reptile house at a zoo. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to the new Reptile House. I'm Rachel, one of the keepers. Please look at the plan in your guide. We're at the entrance, at the bottom, and the main corridor runs straight ahead of us.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Just inside the entrance, on the left of the corridor, is the gift shop. I'd leave it until the end of your visit, or you'll be carrying your souvenirs round with you.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Now, the rooms. On the left, the first room, the one nearest the entrance, is the crocodile pool. Above it is the rainforest room, which is hot and humid, and at the top on the left is the desert room, which is dry but very bright.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: On the right, the room nearest the entrance is our education room, where we run workshops and talks. Above it, in the middle on the right, you'll find the snake gallery. And at the top on the right, there's the tortoise garden, which is open to the sky.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Some background. The Reptile House cost five million pounds to build. Most of that was raised by donations, and the rest came from the zoo's own funds.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Please do take photographs, but without flash. Some people think that flash only spoils the pictures, but it can harm the eyes of some of our animals, especially the nocturnal ones.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: In the tortoise garden, you'll meet Sampson. Nobody knows exactly how old he is, but he is believed to be about a hundred and twenty. He was brought here from a private collection, and he is very friendly.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Every day at two o'clock, one of the keepers gives a talk in the education room. The crocodile feeding is later, at four, and it's best to arrive early to get a good view.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: And on Saturdays, children under twelve can hold a corn snake, with a keeper beside them. It's very popular, so come early. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Research on remote learning
parts.context: Two sociology students discuss the findings of their interviews on remote learning.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two sociology students, Zara and Tim, discussing their research on remote learning. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: Tim, did you get through all the interviews? We only have two days before the draft is due.

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Nearly. I've done eighteen, and three more are booked for tomorrow.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: And how did you find the participants?

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Through the school newsletter, but only parents replied. For the students, I had to go to a youth club and ask there.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: I've been coding the transcripts with the categories we agreed. There's a problem with 'wellbeing'. It's too broad.

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Let's split it into two: social wellbeing and mental health.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: That's better. What about the quotations? Some of them are very long.

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Shorten them, but never change the words. And ask permission if the participant could be recognised.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: One more thing. Dr Rahman suggested that we include a section on limitations.

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Yes. Our sample is small, and all from one town, so we can't say that the results apply everywhere.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: Let's go through the findings group by group. Parents first.

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Many said they had to give up working time to supervise their children, so for them it increased their workload, especially with more than one child.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: Teachers?

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Nearly all of them complained that the technology was unreliable, with connections dropping in the middle of lessons.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: Older students?

script.speaker: tim
script.text: They were positive. They liked the flexibility, being able to watch recorded lessons whenever they wanted.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: And the younger children?

script.speaker: tim
script.text: Mostly they said they felt lonely. They missed their friends, and some of them said they missed the playground more than the lessons.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: And the managers?

script.speaker: tim
script.text: They said it was too expensive, because of the cost of laptops and software licences. None of them said it saved time, which surprised me.

script.speaker: zara
script.text: That's a good point to finish on. I'll write the summary.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: tulip mania
parts.context: An economics lecture on the Dutch tulip bubble of the sixteen thirties.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about tulip mania in the Netherlands. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's topic is one of the most famous episodes in economic history: tulip mania in the Netherlands in the sixteen thirties.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Tulips arrived in Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century, and they quickly became a status symbol for wealthy Dutch merchants. The most prized flowers had flames of colour on the petals. We now know that these were caused by a virus, which also weakened the bulb, so the finest tulips were extremely rare.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The setting matters. This was the Dutch Golden Age, when the country had grown rich from trade, and many people had money to spend.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the early sixteen thirties, ordinary people began to speculate. Bulbs could only be lifted from the ground in summer, so trading moved to contracts for bulbs that were still underground. These contracts were bought and sold in taverns, and buyers did not have to pay at once. They only signed a note.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Prices rose steeply. A single bulb of the most famous variety, called Semper Augustus, is said to have cost as much as a large house in Amsterdam.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Then, in February sixteen thirty-seven, at an auction in Haarlem, the buyers simply failed to appear. The news spread, and within a few days, prices had collapsed.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The traditional story says that thousands were ruined. But modern historians have looked at the court records and found very few disputes, which suggests the crash was much less damaging than people believed. The story was kept alive by moralists, who used it as a warning against greed.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Whatever the truth, the word bubble is still used today for prices that have lost touch with real value. Next week we'll look at the South Sea Company.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
